newsitem.title: HONG KONG: RESEARCH ALERT - Salomon sees hard time for Hopewell.
newsitem.headline: RESEARCH ALERT - Salomon sees hard time for Hopewell.

text.p: Earnings recovery at Hopewell Holdings Ltd is expected to be difficult to achieve and investors should use any strength in the share price to divest, Salomon Brothers said in a report dated October 22.

It said while the sale of a large part of Hopewell's stake in Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd (CEPA) should reduce the company's gearing to 23 percent from 90 percent, it expects the gearing to rebound to about 60 percent in the next nine to 12 months. Salomon maintains an underperform rating on the stock.
"Hopewell's road to recovery is likely to be difficult and fraught with pitfalls," the report said.

It said Hopewell was exposed to large capital outlays and needs to raise capital. "Both factors will have a large impact on the small and rapidly diminishing recurrent earnings base," Salomon analyst Michael Green said in the report.

Hopewell posted fiscal 1996 net profit of HK$769.19 million compared with HK$2.1 billion a year earlier. "Earnings are only 44 percent of the most recent consensus forecast. This supports our suspicion that the company is in a worse financial condition than is generally believed," Salomon said.
Salomon forecasts fiscal 1997 profit of HK$3.69 billion but a fall to HK$1.64 billion in 1998 and to HK$487 million in 1999.
It said if Hopewell continues its 1995/96 rate of spending, it will only be able to fund itself for another nine to 12 months before a large cash infusion will be necessary.

It said Hopewell was also likely to dispose of assets earlier than Salomon had expected before the release of results, with banks expected to be more cautious in lending to Hopewell and the firm's credit rating likely to come under scrutiny.

"The disposal of assets could include a spin-off of Hopewell's hotel operation. It is also increasingly likely that it may come to the market for more equity during the next 12 months," Salomon said. -- Hong Kong newsroom (852) 2843 6345
